articles.title: It’s the Filter’s first birthday! 25 things readers loved most this year – and if we still recommend them
articles.summary: In the course of a year, we’ve tested products ranging from instant coffees and cat toys to towels and sleep masks. These are the ones you loved most. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things. The Filter US is turning one.
body: The Filter US is turning one. Over the past year, we have cooked, cleaned, hiked and generally put our homes and bodies through a lot in pursuit of things actually worth buying. We have tested packing cubes on 14 trips, spent 63 nights testing sleep masks, recruited 84 coffee drinkers to taste instant coffee and put thousands of products through their paces (and called out ones which we don’t recommend ).

And we have gone deeper: asking a food lab to test the best non-toxic pans, blind-tasting everything from protein bars to nonalcoholic beer and getting the tea on Padma Lakshmi’s favorite kitchen tools. Across hundreds of articles, we have covered everything from a satisfyingly bouncy $1,600 organic mattress to a small but mighty $9 cleaning brush. We have found the legitimately best deals on our favorite things too.

One year in, we wanted to know which things should earn a permanent place in your homes. So we pulled the 25 items our readers have loved most since the Filter US launched – then went back to the writers who originally tested them. Did the products survive months of real life? Would our testers still recommend them to you?

articles.title: My relationship with food was broken. Then I killed my own dinner
articles.summary: For years, eating was something to control, fear or regret. After I hunted my first deer, I started to see fat, hunger and my own body in a different light. I muffled my sobs with a pillow so my family couldn’t hear me from the adjacent room.
body: Pulling tear-soaked strands of hair off my cheeks, I stood in front of a full-length mirror and grabbed the fat of my thighs. If only I could just – I pictured ripping off fistfuls of my body and flinging them out the windows, where they would land on some unknowing French person six stories below. I had this vision often: pulling bits of myself off and casting them somewhere far away from me.

For years, spanning my teens and 20s, eating was either an indulgence to regret or a strategy to overplan. In high school, I chugged 32 ounces of cold green tea every morning, hoping it would burn belly fat like Instagram told me it would. While working at a deli one summer, I ate two bagel sandwiches each shift until my friend mentioned I was eating the carbohydrate equivalent of 10 slices of bread. My daily bagel intake promptly plummeted to zero. I forced myself to choke down a can of tuna in my college dorm before predawn weightlifting sessions. In my early 20s, I started experimenting with intermittent fasting: no food from 8pm until noon the next day.
points: For years, eating was something to control, fear or regret.
After I hunted my first deer, I started to see fat, hunger and my own body in a different light.

articles.title: After a Decade-Plus of Chasing Trends, I Finally Found My Uniform on Savile Row
articles.summary: My goal: a single garment to get me through formal occasions during the festive season, rather than multiple evening dresses which take up precious New York City closet real estate.
body: My immersion into the menswear landscape happened fast. Within a couple of weeks of accepting a job overseeing the beat for a luxury title—after more than a decade covering womenswear—I was bound for Pitti Uomo. A biannual industry trade show, Pitti has outgrown the walls of the fortezza that houses it, spilling into the narrow streets of Florence in an influencer-heavy scene of suiting aficionados determined to out-peacock each other—100-plus-degree temps in June be damned. But among the occasionally over-the-top spectacles, an invaluable sartorial shift occurred.

I’d long been drawn to tailoring when wanting to feel particularly pulled together, no doubt a result of the ease of the school uniform I donned during my youth. As a fashion journalist, then so focused on writing about trends, I couldn’t fathom having the time or inclination to embrace suiting. Even so, I was far more likely to pair a blazer with jeans. A full suit? It felt wildly archaic and, if I’m being frank, a bit boring.

articles.title: ‘I waited patiently, hoping he might make the jump’: Mirna Abass’s best phone picture
articles.summary: As a fan of Henri Cartier-Bresson, the Egyptian photographer was determined to capture his own ‘decisive moment’ Mirna Abass regards his small Egyptian city as “heaven for street, travel and documentary photography”.
body: On the day he took this shot, Abass had joined a walk with the Egyptian Camera Crew photography club. Abass works as an agricultural engineer, but describes film and photography as his true passions. Henri Cartier-Bresson is one of his biggest inspirations, and he is often guided by the pioneering photographer’s concept of the decisive moment.

“As we explored the shipyard, I saw this teenage fisher jumping between several boats,” Abass says. “I set up my iPhone 13 to capture these two contrasting boats, side by side, and waited patiently, hoping he might eventually make the jump in front of me. I was elated when he did, and went to show him our very own decisive moment.

“The human element gave a sense of scale, of how large these ships are, and I loved how I captured him leaping from the white ship to the colourful ship,” he adds. “It is almost as if he is escaping from pale life to fruitful life.”

articles.title: Fashion designer Henry Holland: ‘I’ve thought about a nose job but everyone says I’ll look different. That’s the point!’
articles.summary: Holland on his dashed Olympic dreams, ranking the Real Housewives shows, and a terrifying taxi ride. Born in Greater Manchester, Henry Holland, 43, worked as a stylist and fashion editor for Smash Hits magazine.
body: When were you happiest? In my late teen years, on that verge of having independence and no responsibilities.
What is your greatest fear? Going through grief and the loss of a parent was one of the toughest things I’ve ever done, so it happening again is my biggest fear.
What is your most treasured possession? This chain I wear round my neck, which was my mum’s.
What is your guiltiest pleasure? The Real Housewives – all franchises but primarily Salt Lake City, Beverly Hills and Orange County.

articles.title: Katseye’s Lara and Megan Bring Bestie Style to Their First-Ever Paris Fashion Week Show
articles.summary: Loewe’s spring 2027 show was a big day for one very special duo. Yes, designers Jack McCullough and Lazaro Hernandez, but also Katseye’s Lara Raj and Megan Skiendiel.
body: The two best friends took opposite approaches to their Loewe show looks. “Recently I’ve been loving bright colors,” says Lara, whose canary leather halter dress fit right into her personal style brief: “sexy, bold, regal, and risqué.” (Megan concurs, deeming Lara “glamorous, extravagant, and classy.”) Still, she admits, the yellow dress felt like “a big risk.” It paid off. “The dress reminded me of sunshine, and I felt it would go well with the castle setting of the show. It made me feel very beautiful.” she adds. “I love bold colors and I love how it complemented my skin tone.”

Megan, who describes her go-to look as “effortlessly edgy,” took a different route in a slouchy brown blouse with a plunging neckline, a black pleated leather skirt, cutout mules, and—for a pop of color—a vibrant teal Whisker bag. “The blend between the masculine and feminine drew me to my outfit,” Megan tells Vogue. “I thought it was so edgy and cool. When I saw it on the rack I immediately wanted to put it on. It excited me.” Lara adds: “Megan is very effortless and chic and sleek. Her style always inspires me to be more chic.”
points: Loewe’s spring 2027 show was a big day for one very special duo.

articles.title: Could “Dry Conditioning” Give You Healthier, Shinier Hair?
articles.summary: Hairstylist Xavier Velasquez is a fan of the trend—which can help maintain color on dyed hair and cause less frizz!—but says it’s not for everybody.
body: It appears to be part of the human condition: We will never stop looking for a way to get shinier, stronger, healthier hair. And social media seems to always have a theory: hair tonics, rosemary oil, and water temperature … The latest theory? It’s called “dry conditioning.”

“Dry conditioning is when you apply conditioning treatment on last-day hair right before you wash it,” says hairstylist Xavier Velasquez, cofounder of the Manhattan salon Franklin’s. Yes, dry conditioning is a step you do before you hop in the shower when hair is still dry—leave it in for however long the mask says—then shower like you normally would. “It will create a barrier on your strands so you don’t over tangle in the shower.” He adds that this is meant to protect and hydrate the parts of hair that oil doesn’t typically reach, so you should focus on the mid-shaft to ends when trying the trend.
points: Hairstylist Xavier Velasquez is a fan of the trend—which can help maintain color on dyed hair and cause less frizz!—but says it’s not for everybody.

articles.title: Hailey Bieber Finally Gets the ‘French Show With the Good Lighting’ Treatment
articles.summary: Hailey Bieber put Quotidien’s famously flattering lighting to the ultimate test—with a first look at what might be Rhode’s next big beauty launch.
body: There are certain rites of passage for the modern celebrity: the Met Gala steps, a Hot Ones interrogation, a turn in the Vogue Beauty Secrets bathroom. And, increasingly, there is “the French show with the good lighting.”

The show in question is Quotidien, the daily French news and culture program hosted by Yann Barthès on TMC, which has acquired an unlikely second life online thanks to its almost preternaturally flattering studio lighting. Clips of Margot Robbie, Zendaya, Sabrina Carpenter, Timothée Chalamet, and others sitting beneath its warm glow have ricocheted around social media, where viewers have become fascinated by the way everyone seems to emerge looking particularly luminous. Zara Larsson has even publicly campaigned for an appearance, while Sombr referenced the nickname when he finally made it onto the show. Now, Hailey Bieber has entered the chat.
points: Hailey Bieber put Quotidien’s famously flattering lighting to the ultimate test—with a first look at what might be Rhode’s next big beauty launch.

body: Style in NYC has never really been about following one formula, nor should you when walking in this kaleidoscopic of a city. Whether you’re checking out a new museum exhibition, plotting a night out on Broadway, or simply looking for some fall fashion inspiration, these outfits have you covered for a trip to the Big Apple, mixing timeless New York style with the trends that make it all feel fresh.
Consider this a suitcase of reasons to get dressed up in New York City. No matter what’s on the agenda this season, here’s what to wear in the city that never sleeps.

While there’s no official dress code for Broadway, it’s a special night on the town—and you might want to plan for dinner and a drink beforehand, making it a perfect excuse to look a little spiffy. There’s plenty on Broadway right now, from Wicked and Hamilton to Buena Vista Social Club and MJ The Musical. Just make sure your look is comfortable enough for a couple of hours in your seat.

articles.title: A Fall-Lover's Guide to Visiting Salem, Massachusetts, the US's Real-Life Halloweentown
articles.summary: The historic city turns 400 this year—here's how to experience its milestone fall.
body: I love everything about fall: the crisp weather, the changing leaves, the pumpkin spice, the apple picking, and—above all else— Halloween. The haunted holiday is my Super Bowl (I start thinking about what to wear next year on November 1), so it should come as no surprise that I've graced the streets of Salem, Massachusetts, quite a few times.

I've enjoyed my trips to the historic city about 45 minutes from Boston in every season, but due to my proclivities for all things ghostly, my most recent visit was last year during October: the city's high season. Famous for its 17th-century witch trials, in which hundreds of people were accused of witchcraft in Puritan Massachusetts and put to a notoriously unfair trial, the city has gained a reputation for haunted thrills, offering museums that let guests explore the infamous history as well as more upbeat Halloween-themed events all October long.
points: The historic city turns 400 this year—here's how to experience its milestone fall.
